condition: Malrotation with volvulus mislabelled as reflux
permutationLabel: 3-week-old on Gaviscon for "reflux", green vomits today, well-looking
summary: 3-week-old boy (3.9 kg) diagnosed with reflux last week and started on Gaviscon; today three green vomits (parents show a photo), irritable but well-perfused, abdomen soft. The "reflux" label and a benign examination must not delay the contrast study.

inputs.chiefComplaint: Reflux getting worse — vomit now green
inputs.hpi: 3-week-old boy seen last week for posseting and "reflux", started on Gaviscon Infant. Today three vomits that were green (parents have a photo of dark green vomit). Irritable, feeding less. Stools normal yesterday. No fever.

exam.general: Irritable but consolable, well-perfused. T 36.8, HR 160, RR 42, CRT < 2 s.
exam.abdomen: Soft, not distended, not tender. Normal anus. No hernias.

confirmedDiagnosis.name: Bilious vomiting in a neonate — malrotation with volvulus to be excluded
confirmedDiagnosis.assessmentText: Green vomiting in a 3-week-old: not reflux. Emergency upper GI contrast study and immediate paediatric surgical referral; NBM, NG tube, IV fluids.

mustNotMiss.knownGapNote: PANE has no malrotation/midgut volvulus disease node (pane-engine has 130 diseases, none for malrotation/midgut volvulus); top 3: GORD (the relief answer "Gaviscon — no help" still sets antacid_relief), inguinal hernia, cholecystitis. Symptom inference ranks malrotation #1 (secondary view).
mustNotMiss.proposedFix: Add paediatric surgical conditions (intussusception, pyloric stenosis, malrotation/volvulus) as PANE nodes and management protocols (Q40.0, Q43.3, K56.1) with paediatric surgery referral. Bilious-vomiting hard rule; negation-aware relief parsing.

emergencyLevel.note: A normal examination does not exclude volvulus.

mustExclude.note: The reflux label must not be reinforced by the plan.

Weight 3.9 kg. Paracetamol 1 g, ibuprofen 400 mg, piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g, co-amoxiclav 1.2 g, meropenem 1 g, morphine 2.5–5 mg, ondansetron 4 mg and fixed 1 L, 1–2 L or 500 mL fluid volumes are adult fixed doses; a child needs weight-based (mg/kg, mL/kg) dosing. Prescribing accuracy is a patient-safety issue, so critical.

An ACS, PE or AF antithrombotic/thrombolytic plan must never be attached to this diagnosis. Regression guard: before 999f838 (word-boundary lookup) "mi" inside "vomiting" would have attached the ACS plan (aspirin 300 mg, ticagrelor, fondaparinux) to a neonate. With word-boundary matching the diagnosis matches the adult small-bowel-obstruction entry ("volvulus"), which has no antithrombotic content (simulated from the source); to be confirmed on the first iOS CI run.

guideline.name: Intestinal rotation abnormalities and midgut volvulus
guideline.section: Bilious vomiting in a neonate/infant is malrotation with midgut volvulus until proven otherwise: emergency upper GI contrast study and immediate paediatric surgical assessment (Ladd procedure); delay risks loss of the midgut
guideline.citation: Langer JC. Intestinal rotation abnormalities and midgut volvulus. Surg Clin North Am. 2017;97:147–159.

guideline.name: ACR Appropriateness Criteria — vomiting in infants
guideline.section: Non-bilious projectile vomiting (suspected hypertrophic pyloric stenosis): ultrasound of the pylorus; bilious vomiting in an infant: upper GI contrast series (malrotation/midgut volvulus) as a surgical emergency
guideline.citation: Expert Panel on Pediatric Imaging; Alazraki AL, Rigsby CK, Iyer RS, et al. ACR Appropriateness Criteria® Vomiting in Infants. J Am Coll Radiol. 2020;17:S505–S515.

rationale: Anchoring on a prior "reflux" diagnosis is a known cause of delayed volvulus diagnosis. The colour of the vomit, not the examination, drives the emergency pathway.
